questions.q: What is the main objective of a commercial organisation?
o: Providing free services to its members
Promoting a religious or cultural cause
Earning profit by supplying goods or services
questions.why: A commercial organisation exists to earn profit; serving members or a cause without profit is the aim of a non-commercial organisation.

questions.q: Which of these is a non-commercial organisation?
o: A charitable hospital run by a trust
questions.why: A charitable hospital aims at service to society, not profit, so it is non-commercial.

questions.q: A non-commercial organisation such as a sports club gets most of its funds from
o: selling shares on the stock exchange
profits from buying and selling goods
interest on loans given to the public
questions.why: Non-commercial bodies depend on members' subscriptions, donations and government grants rather than trading profits.

questions.q: Which department of a commercial organisation raises funds and keeps a record of all money received and paid?
questions.why: The finance and accounts department manages funds and records every receipt and payment.

questions.q: When a non-commercial organisation's income exceeds its expenditure, the excess (surplus) is
o: divided among the members as dividend
paid to the government as a penalty
used to further the organisation's aims
treated as the secretary's personal income
questions.why: A non-commercial organisation does not distribute surplus to members; it ploughs it back into its objectives.

long.q: Distinguish between a commercial and a non-commercial organisation on the basis of (a) objective and (b) source of funds.
scheme: B1: (a) Commercial organisation: aims at earning profit.
B1: (a) Non-commercial organisation: aims at service or welfare of members or society.
B1: (b) Commercial organisation: funds come from owners' capital, loans and sale proceeds.
B1: (b) Non-commercial organisation: funds come from subscriptions, donations, grants and fees.

long.q: Apart from earning profit, state any three objectives of a commercial organisation.
scheme: B1: Survival: to stay in business and remain stable over a long period.
B1: Growth: to expand sales, output, branches or markets.
B1: Any one more, explained: customer satisfaction, innovation, employee welfare, goodwill or social responsibility.

long.q: Name any four functional departments of a manufacturing company and state one function of each.
scheme: B1: Purchase: buys raw materials and other inputs of the right quality at the right price and time.
B1: Production: converts raw materials into finished goods and controls quality.
B1: Marketing / sales: finds customers' needs, promotes and sells the products.
B1: Finance and accounts (or human resource): raises and controls funds and keeps accounts (or recruits, trains and pays staff).

long.q: Give two reasons why a trust-run hospital, which does not aim at profit, must still manage its funds carefully.
scheme: B1: Its income from donations and grants is limited and uncertain, so wasting it would stop essential services.
B1: It is accountable to donors, members and the government for how money is spent, and must keep proper records.

long.q: The Kolkata Book Lovers' Society runs a free reading room. Last year it collected ₹1,20,000 as subscriptions and donations and spent ₹95,000. (a) Is it a commercial or a non-commercial organisation? Give a reason. (b) What is the excess of ₹25,000 called, and how should it be used? (c) State two ways in which the Society differs from a bookshop in the same street.
scheme: B1: (a) Non-commercial organisation.
B1: (a) Its aim is to serve its members and readers, not to earn profit.
B1: (b) It is a surplus (excess of income over expenditure): ₹1,20,000 − ₹95,000 = ₹25,000.
B1: (b) It is used to further the Society's aims, e.g. buying more books; it is not shared among members.
B1: (c) The bookshop aims at profit; the Society aims at service.
B1: (c) The bookshop earns from selling books; the Society depends on subscriptions and donations.
long.ans: Non-commercial; a surplus of ₹25,000, used for the Society's aims

questions.q: A stakeholder of a commercial organisation is
o: only a person who holds its shares
any person or group that affects, or is affected by, its activities
only a member of its board of directors
only the government department that taxes it
questions.why: Stakeholders include owners, employees, customers, suppliers, the government and society: anyone with an interest in the firm's activities.

questions.q: Which of these is an internal stakeholder?
questions.why: Owners, managers and employees work within the organisation; customers, suppliers and the community are outside it.

questions.q: What do customers mainly expect from a commercial organisation?
o: Good-quality goods at fair prices with proper after-sales service
Payment of taxes on their behalf
questions.why: Customers want value for money: quality, fair price and service. Dividends go to shareholders and wages to employees.

questions.q: Suppliers of raw materials to a business mainly expect
o: voting rights at the annual general meeting
regular orders and timely payment of their dues
free advertisement of their own products
questions.why: Suppliers want steady business and prompt payment; bonus is an employee expectation and voting rights belong to shareholders.

questions.q: The government expects a commercial organisation to
o: pay its taxes honestly and obey the laws of the country
sell all its goods below cost
questions.why: The government expects lawful conduct and honest tax payment, which fund public services.

long.q: Distinguish between internal and external stakeholders, giving two examples of each.
scheme: B1: Internal stakeholders are within the organisation and directly take part in running it.
B1: Examples: owners/shareholders, managers, employees (any two).
B1: External stakeholders are outside the organisation but are affected by its decisions.
B1: Examples: customers, suppliers, creditors, government, society (any two).

long.q: State two expectations of employees from the organisation they work for.
scheme: B1: Fair and timely wages, with bonus and other benefits.
B1: Safe working conditions, job security, training and chances of promotion (any one).

long.q: State two responsibilities of a commercial organisation towards the society in which it operates.
scheme: B1: Avoid pollution and protect the environment, e.g. treating waste before release.
B1: Generate local employment or support community welfare such as schools and health camps (CSR activities).

long.q: Explain how the interests of owners and employees of a company may conflict, and suggest one way to reduce the conflict.
scheme: B1: Owners want higher profits, so they try to keep costs, including wages, low.
B1: Employees want higher wages and more benefits, which raise costs and reduce profit.
B1: Remedy: link bonus or incentives to productivity, or settle wages through regular discussion with workers.

long.q: A cement factory near Satna plans to double its output. Explain how this decision is likely to affect (a) its shareholders, (b) the local residents and (c) the government. Give one benefit and one concern for each.
scheme: B1: (a) Benefit: higher sales may raise profits and dividends.
B1: (a) Concern: more capital is needed and the expansion carries risk if demand falls.
B1: (b) Benefit: more jobs and business for local people.
B1: (b) Concern: more dust, traffic and pollution may harm health.
B1: (c) Benefit: more tax revenue (GST, income tax).
B1: (c) Concern: it must ensure the factory follows pollution and safety laws.

questions.q: When does marketing begin?
o: Only after the goods have been produced
Only when sales start to fall
After the goods have been delivered to the buyer
Before production, by finding out what customers want
questions.why: Marketing starts with identifying customer needs and continues after sale; selling begins only after goods are made.

questions.q: Selling mainly focuses on
o: persuading buyers so that goods are converted into cash
questions.why: Selling is product-centred and aims at transferring ownership for money; customer research and satisfaction belong to marketing.

questions.q: The four Ps of the marketing mix are
questions.why: The marketing mix is the combination of product, price, place (distribution) and promotion.

questions.q: Market research means
o: collecting and analysing information about customers, competitors and the market
fixing prices by a government order
opening a shop in a busy market
questions.why: Market research gathers facts on what buyers want and what rivals offer, so that decisions are based on evidence.

questions.q: In the marketing mix, 'Place' refers to
o: the location of the company's head office
the channels through which the product reaches customers
the price of the land the factory stands on
the city where the goods are manufactured
questions.why: Place covers distribution: wholesalers, retailers, online stores and transport that get the product to buyers.

long.q: Distinguish between marketing and selling on any three bases.
scheme: B1: Scope: marketing is wider and includes selling; selling is only one part of marketing.
B1: Focus: marketing focuses on customers' needs; selling focuses on the product already made.
B1: Time: marketing starts before production; selling starts after production.
B1: Its second side made clear for the time basis (marketing continues after the sale; selling ends with it).
B1: Objective: marketing earns profit through customer satisfaction; selling through the volume of sales.
B1: Its second side made clear for the objective basis (satisfaction builds repeat customers; selling seeks immediate cash).

long.q: State any four functions of marketing.
scheme: B1: Market research: finding out customers' needs.
B1: Product planning and development, including packaging and branding.
B1: Pricing: fixing a price that suits buyers and covers costs.
B1: Distribution and promotion: getting the goods to buyers and informing them (advertising, sales promotion).

long.q: What is meant by 'consumer orientation' in marketing? Give an example.
scheme: B1: The business first studies what consumers need and then produces goods to satisfy those needs.
B1: Example: a company launching smaller, cheaper sachets of shampoo because rural buyers want low-priced packs.

long.q: A company in Pune wants to launch a low-sugar fruit juice for health-conscious buyers. Explain how it should decide on each element of the marketing mix.
scheme: B1: Product: low-sugar juice in hygienic, attractive packs of suitable sizes with a clear label.
B1: Price: a price that health-conscious buyers will pay, considering cost and rival brands.
B1: Place: sell through supermarkets, gyms, chemists and online stores where such buyers shop.
B1: Promotion: advertise the health benefit, e.g. on social media, with free tasting at stores.

long.q: Give two reasons why market research is important before launching a new product.
scheme: B1: It shows whether there is enough demand, reducing the risk of failure.
B1: It helps decide features, price and promotion that customers prefer, and shows what rivals offer.

questions.q: Instructions passed from a manager to the workers under him are an example of
questions.why: Communication from a superior to subordinates flows downward.

questions.q: The informal channel of communication in an organisation is called
questions.why: The grapevine spreads through informal, personal contact; the scalar chain, memos and circulars are formal.

questions.q: Feedback in the communication process is
o: the original idea in the sender's mind
the receiver's response, which tells the sender whether the message was understood
the medium through which the message travels
the noise that distorts the message
questions.why: Feedback completes the process by showing the sender how the message was received.

questions.q: Which of these is a language (semantic) barrier to communication?
o: Staff hesitating to speak to a senior officer
Using technical terms that the receiver does not understand
questions.why: Semantic barriers arise from words and meanings; noise and faulty lines are physical, and hesitation before seniors is a status barrier.

questions.q: Which form of communication is best when a message must be kept as a legal record?
questions.why: A written message can be filed and produced later as proof.

long.q: Explain the process of communication by stating its elements in the correct order.
scheme: B1: The sender has an idea and encodes it into words, symbols or signs.
B1: The message is sent through a channel or medium (letter, phone, e-mail, meeting).
B1: The receiver receives and decodes (interprets) the message.
B1: The receiver gives feedback to the sender, completing the process.

long.q: Distinguish between formal and informal communication on any two bases.
scheme: B1: Channel: formal communication follows the official chain of authority.
B1: Informal communication moves through personal contacts and has no fixed path.
B1: Record and reliability: formal communication is usually written and reliable.
B1: Informal communication is mostly oral, fast, and may carry rumours that are hard to verify.

long.q: State two merits and one demerit of oral communication.
scheme: B1: Merit: quick, saves time and allows immediate feedback.
B1: Merit: personal and flexible; doubts can be cleared on the spot.
B1: Demerit: no permanent record, so it is not useful as legal proof or for lengthy messages.

long.q: Explain any three barriers to effective communication and suggest one way to overcome each.
scheme: B1: Semantic barrier: unclear words or jargon.
B1: Remedy: use simple, clear language suited to the receiver.
B1: Physical barrier: noise, distance or faulty equipment.
B1: Remedy: choose a quiet place or a reliable medium and check equipment.
B1: Psychological/status barrier: fear of seniors, lack of attention or distrust.
B1: Remedy: encourage an open-door policy and active listening; seek feedback.

long.q: What is horizontal communication? Give one example.
scheme: B1: Communication between people at the same level of authority, usually in different departments.
B1: Example: the production manager discussing a delivery schedule with the sales manager.

topics.name: Fundamentals of Accounting and the Journal

questions.q: The rule for debiting and crediting a personal account is
o: debit what comes in, credit what goes out
debit the receiver, credit the giver
debit all expenses and losses, credit all incomes and gains
debit the giver, credit the receiver
questions.why: Personal accounts follow 'debit the receiver, credit the giver'; the other rules are for real and nominal accounts.

questions.q: Goods worth ₹5,000 were bought for cash. Which journal entry is correct?
o: Purchases A/c Dr ₹5,000; To Cash A/c ₹5,000
Cash A/c Dr ₹5,000; To Purchases A/c ₹5,000
Purchases A/c Dr ₹5,000; To Capital A/c ₹5,000
Sales A/c Dr ₹5,000; To Cash A/c ₹5,000
questions.why: Purchases (an expense) are debited and Cash, which goes out, is credited.

questions.q: A trader's assets are ₹2,50,000 and his liabilities are ₹90,000. What is his capital?
questions.why: Capital = Assets − Liabilities = ₹2,50,000 − ₹90,000 = ₹1,60,000.

questions.q: Rent paid for the shop is recorded in which type of account?
questions.why: Expenses, losses, incomes and gains are nominal accounts.

questions.q: In accounting, 'drawings' means
o: cash or goods taken by the owner from the business for personal use
plans and sketches of the business premises
questions.why: Drawings reduce the owner's capital; they are not a business expense.

long.q: Journalise the following transactions in the books of Riya Traders: (a) Started business with cash ₹1,00,000. (b) Bought goods on credit from Mohan ₹20,000. (c) Sold goods for cash ₹15,000. (d) Paid salary ₹6,000.
scheme: B1: (a) Cash A/c Dr ₹1,00,000; To Capital A/c ₹1,00,000.
B1: (b) Purchases A/c Dr ₹20,000; To Mohan ₹20,000.
B1: (c) Cash A/c Dr ₹15,000; To Sales A/c ₹15,000.
B1: (d) Salary A/c Dr ₹6,000; To Cash A/c ₹6,000.

long.q: State the principle of double entry.
scheme: B1: Every transaction has two aspects, affecting at least two accounts.
B1: One account is debited and another credited with an equal amount, so total debits equal total credits.

long.q: Explain the following accounting terms: (a) assets, (b) liabilities, (c) capital.
scheme: B1: (a) Assets: things of value owned by the business, e.g. machinery, stock, cash, debtors.
B1: (b) Liabilities: amounts the business owes to outsiders, e.g. creditors, bank loan.
B1: (c) Capital: the amount invested by the owner; the business owes it to the owner.

long.q: Classify the following accounts as personal, real or nominal: (a) Machinery, (b) Ravi, (c) Wages, (d) State Bank of India, (e) Commission received, (f) Building.
scheme: B1: (a) Machinery: real.
B1: (b) Ravi: personal (natural).
B1: (c) Wages: nominal.
B1: (d) State Bank of India: personal (artificial).
B1: (e) Commission received: nominal.
B1: (f) Building: real.

long.q: Anil started business with cash ₹50,000. He then bought furniture for cash ₹10,000 and goods on credit from Amit ₹8,000. Show the accounting equation after all three transactions.
scheme: A1: Assets: Cash ₹40,000 + Furniture ₹10,000 + Stock ₹8,000 = ₹58,000.
B1: Liabilities: Creditor (Amit) ₹8,000; Capital ₹50,000.
A1: Assets ₹58,000 = Liabilities ₹8,000 + Capital ₹50,000.

topics.name: Ledger, Cash Book and Trial Balance

questions.q: A trial balance is prepared mainly to
o: find the net profit of the year
show the financial position on a date
check the arithmetical accuracy of the ledger postings
questions.why: If the debit and credit totals agree, the ledger is arithmetically accurate; profit and position come from final accounts.

questions.q: A ledger account has a debit total of ₹18,000 and a credit total of ₹11,000. Its balance is
questions.why: ₹18,000 − ₹11,000 = ₹7,000; the larger side is debit, so it is a debit balance (written as balance c/d on the credit side).

questions.q: Which error is NOT revealed by a trial balance?
o: A transaction completely left out of the books
Wrong totalling of a ledger account
An amount posted to the wrong side of an account
Posting only one side of an entry
questions.why: An error of omission affects neither side, so the trial balance still agrees.

questions.q: A simple (single-column) cash book records
o: only cash receipts and cash payments
questions.why: A simple cash book has one cash column; credit transactions and depreciation are not cash.

questions.q: Why can the cash column of a cash book never show a credit balance?
o: Cash paid out can never be more than the cash available
Cash account is a nominal account
Credit balances are carried to the Profit and Loss Account
The cash book is not part of the ledger
questions.why: One cannot spend more cash than one has; the cash book also serves as the cash account in the ledger.

long.q: Prepare a Cash Account from the following and balance it: Capital introduced ₹60,000; goods bought for cash ₹25,000; goods sold for cash ₹18,000; rent paid ₹4,000.
scheme: M1: Debit side: To Capital ₹60,000 and To Sales ₹18,000 (total ₹78,000).
M1: Credit side: By Purchases ₹25,000 and By Rent ₹4,000.
A1: By Balance c/d ₹49,000 (₹78,000 − ₹29,000), both sides totalling ₹78,000.
B1: To Balance b/d ₹49,000 shown on the debit side at the start of the next period.

long.q: From the following balances, find the cash balance and prepare a trial balance: Capital ₹80,000; Furniture ₹20,000; Purchases ₹45,000; Sales ₹60,000; Debtors ₹15,000; Creditors ₹10,000; Salaries ₹8,000; Cash ? (the trial balance agrees).
scheme: B1: Debit items: Furniture, Purchases, Debtors, Salaries and Cash.
B1: Credit items: Capital, Sales and Creditors, totalling ₹1,50,000.
A1: Cash balance = ₹62,000.
A1: Both columns total ₹1,50,000.

long.q: Distinguish between a journal and a ledger on any two bases.
scheme: B1: Nature: the journal is the book of original (first) entry.
B1: The ledger is the book of final entry, which receives postings from the journal.
B1: Arrangement: the journal records transactions in date (chronological) order.
B1: The ledger groups them account-wise and shows the balance of each account.

long.q: State two limitations of a trial balance.
scheme: B1: It does not reveal errors of omission or errors of principle (e.g. a capital item posted as revenue).
B1: It does not reveal compensating errors or entries posted to the wrong account on the correct side.

long.q: What is meant by balancing an account? How is a debit balance shown?
scheme: B1: Balancing means finding the difference between the two sides of an account and writing it on the shorter side so both totals agree.
B1: A debit balance is written as 'By Balance c/d' on the credit side and brought down as 'To Balance b/d' on the debit side.

questions.q: Which mode of transport is most suitable for carrying coal in bulk from Jharkhand to a power station 900 km away?
questions.why: Railways carry heavy, bulky goods over long distances cheaply.

questions.q: Transport adds value to goods by creating
questions.why: Moving goods from where they are plentiful to where they are needed creates place utility; storage creates time utility.

questions.q: Which is the fastest but costliest mode of transport?
questions.why: Air transport saves time but has high freight charges.

questions.q: Which mode is the cheapest for carrying large volumes of goods between countries?
questions.why: Ships carry huge cargoes at a low cost per tonne, which suits bulk international trade.

questions.q: Which mode of transport offers door-to-door service?
questions.why: Trucks and vans can pick up and deliver at the doorstep; other modes need road transport at both ends.

long.q: State any four points showing the importance of transport in commerce.
scheme: B1: Creates place utility by moving goods to where they are needed.
B1: Widens the market: goods can be sold across the country and abroad.
B1: Helps stabilise prices by moving goods from surplus to shortage areas.
B1: Supports large-scale production and division of labour; helps in emergencies such as floods.

long.q: State two merits and two demerits of rail transport.
scheme: B1: Merit: cheap for heavy and bulky goods over long distances.
B1: Merit: safe, regular and less affected by weather.
B1: Demerit: no door-to-door service; goods need loading and unloading.
B1: Demerit: inflexible routes and timings; not economical for short distances or small loads.

long.q: Give two reasons why pipelines are used to carry petroleum and natural gas.
scheme: B1: Low running cost and continuous, uninterrupted flow once laid.
B1: Safe with little loss in transit; can cross difficult terrain and is not affected by weather.

long.q: Suggest the most suitable mode of transport, with a reason, for each: (a) fresh flowers from Bengaluru to Dubai, (b) iron ore from Odisha's mines to Paradip port, (c) milk from nearby villages to a dairy in the city.
scheme: B1: (a) Air transport.
B1: (a) Flowers are perishable and must reach quickly over a long distance.
B1: (b) Rail transport.
B1: (b) Iron ore is heavy and bulky; railways carry it cheaply over land.
B1: (c) Road transport.
B1: (c) Short distance, door-to-door collection and quick delivery.

long.q: Distinguish between road transport and rail transport on two bases.
scheme: B1: Flexibility: road transport is flexible in routes and timing; rail runs on fixed tracks and timetables.
B1: Suitability: road suits short distances and small loads; rail suits long distances and bulky goods.

questions.q: Warehousing adds value to goods by creating
questions.why: Storing goods until they are needed creates time utility.

questions.q: A bonded warehouse is used to store
o: only perishable goods at low temperature
imported goods on which customs duty has not yet been paid
goods of a single trader free of charge
goods produced by co-operative societies only
questions.why: Bonded warehouses are licensed by the government for imported goods held under bond until duty is paid.

questions.q: Which document issued by a warehouse keeper can be transferred by endorsement to pass ownership of the goods?
questions.why: A warehouse warrant is a document of title to goods; a bill of lading is issued by a shipping company.

questions.q: Cold storage warehouses are most suitable for
questions.why: Perishable goods need low temperatures to stay fresh.

questions.q: Which public body runs warehouses across India for storing food grains and other goods?
o: Securities and Exchange Board of India
questions.why: The Central Warehousing Corporation provides public storage; the others regulate banking, securities and standards.

long.q: State any four functions of warehousing.
scheme: B1: Storage of goods until they are needed.
B1: Price stabilisation by releasing goods when supply is short.
B1: Risk bearing: goods are kept safely and can be insured.
B1: Financing: loans can be raised against warehouse receipts; also grading, packing and processing.

long.q: Distinguish between private and public warehouses on two bases.
scheme: B1: Ownership: private warehouses are owned by manufacturers or traders for their own goods.
B1: Public warehouses are run by the government or licensed operators and are open to anyone on payment of rent.
B1: Cost: private warehouses need heavy investment by the owner.
B1: Public warehouses charge only rent, suit small traders and are regulated by government rules.

long.q: Explain how warehousing helps to keep prices stable.
scheme: B1: Goods produced in bulk in one season (e.g. wheat at harvest) are stored instead of being sold all at once.
B1: They are released when supply falls, so prices neither crash at harvest nor shoot up later.

long.q: State three features of a bonded warehouse.
scheme: B1: Licensed by the government and usually located near ports.
B1: Stores imported goods until customs duty is paid; goods are released only after payment.
B1: Importers can pay duty in instalments as they take out goods, or re-export without paying duty.

long.q: A mango grower in Ratnagiri picks 20 tonnes of mangoes in May. Explain three ways in which a cold-storage warehouse helps him.
scheme: B1: Keeps the mangoes fresh for longer, reducing spoilage.
B1: He need not sell all at once at low prices; he can sell later when prices are better.
B1: He can raise a loan against the warehouse receipt to meet immediate expenses.

questions.q: The principle of utmost good faith requires that
o: the insurer pays double the loss
the insured may hide facts to reduce the premium
both parties disclose all material facts truthfully
only the insurer must be honest
questions.why: Insurance rests on trust; hiding a material fact can make the policy void.

questions.q: Insurable interest means that the insured
o: would suffer a financial loss if the subject matter were damaged
has a friend who owns the property
earns interest from the insurance company
has paid the premium for ten years
questions.why: One can insure only what one would lose money from, such as one's own house or stock.

questions.q: The principle of indemnity does NOT apply to
questions.why: Human life cannot be valued in money, so a life policy pays the sum assured; it is not compensation for an exact loss.

questions.q: Premium is
o: the amount the insurer pays on a claim
the amount paid by the insured to the insurer for the cover
questions.why: The insured pays a premium; in return the insurer promises to pay on the event.

questions.q: Under the principle of subrogation,
o: the insured may claim from two insurers for the same loss
the insured must pay the premium in advance
after paying a claim, the insurer takes over the insured's rights against a third party
the nearest cause of loss is considered
questions.why: Subrogation stops the insured from gaining twice: having been paid, he passes his rights against the wrongdoer to the insurer.

long.q: Explain the principles of (a) indemnity and (b) contribution.
scheme: B1: (a) Indemnity: the insured is compensated only for the actual loss suffered.
B1: (a) He cannot make a profit from insurance; he is put back in the position he was in before the loss.
B1: (b) Contribution: when the same property is insured with more than one insurer, they share the loss.
B1: (b) The insured cannot recover more than the actual loss from all insurers together.

long.q: Distinguish between life insurance and fire insurance on two bases.
scheme: B1: Indemnity: fire insurance is a contract of indemnity; the claim equals the actual loss.
B1: Life insurance is not a contract of indemnity; a fixed sum assured is paid.
B1: Period: fire insurance is usually for one year and renewed.
B1: Life insurance runs for many years or for life, and also has a savings element.

long.q: A shopkeeper in Indore insures his stock, worth ₹8,00,000, against fire for ₹8,00,000. A fire destroys stock worth ₹1,50,000. (a) How much can he claim? (b) Which principle decides this? (c) Can he claim ₹8,00,000? Why?
scheme: B1: (b) The principle of indemnity.
B1: (c) No: insurance only makes good the actual loss; he cannot profit from it.

long.q: State two ways in which insurance helps a business.
scheme: B1: It protects the business against heavy losses from fire, theft or accidents, so it can continue.
B1: It makes it easier to borrow, since banks prefer insured assets, and it encourages taking reasonable risks.

long.q: Explain the principle of causa proxima with an example.
scheme: B1: Causa proxima means the nearest (direct) cause of the loss.
B1: The insurer pays only if the direct cause is a risk covered by the policy.
B1: Example: goods insured against fire are damaged by water used to put out a fire; fire is the proximate cause, so the claim is paid.

questions.q: Advertising is best described as
o: free mention of a firm in a news report
a paid, non-personal presentation of goods, services or ideas by an identified sponsor
giving free samples in a store
questions.why: Advertising is paid for, reaches people through media rather than in person, and names its sponsor.

questions.q: Which advertising medium combines sound and moving pictures to reach a very large audience?
questions.why: Television carries sound and visuals together and reaches homes across the country.

questions.q: Which of these is a criticism of advertising?
o: Its cost may be added to the price of the product
It informs buyers about new products
It creates jobs in the media industry
questions.why: Critics argue that heavy advertising costs are passed on to consumers; the other options are benefits.

questions.q: A government advertisement urging people to wear helmets while riding is an example of
questions.why: It promotes a social message, not a product or a brand.

questions.q: The Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI) is
o: a self-regulatory body that deals with complaints about misleading advertisements
a bank that lends to advertisers
questions.why: ASCI, set up by the advertising industry, checks that advertisements are honest and decent.

long.q: Distinguish between advertising and publicity on two bases.
scheme: B1: Payment: advertising is paid for by the sponsor; publicity is free.
B1: Sponsor: in advertising the sponsor is identified; publicity has no identified sponsor (it comes as news).

long.q: Explain any four objectives of advertising.
scheme: B1: To inform buyers about a new product, its uses and price.
B1: To persuade people to buy and increase sales.
B1: To remind existing customers and keep the brand in their minds.
B1: To build the image and goodwill of the firm and meet competition.

long.q: State two merits and two limitations of advertising in newspapers.
scheme: B1: Merit: wide reach at a relatively low cost; regional papers reach local readers.
B1: Merit: quick to arrange; messages can be changed daily.
B1: Limitation: short life; a newspaper is thrown away the next day.
B1: Limitation: not useful for people who cannot read; pictures may print poorly.

long.q: Give two reasons why advertising is criticised.
scheme: B1: It can mislead buyers with exaggerated or false claims.
B1: It may raise prices or encourage people to buy things they do not need.

long.q: A start-up in Jaipur sells handmade leather footwear online to college students across India. Suggest two suitable advertising media and give a reason for each.
scheme: B1: Social media / internet advertising.
B1: Young buyers spend much time online; ads can be targeted by age and link directly to the online store.
B1: A second suitable medium, e.g. video-sharing platforms, or college magazines and campus events.
B1: A matching reason, e.g. designs can be shown visually, or the target group is reached directly at low cost.

questions.q: Sales promotion techniques are mainly used to
o: increase sales quickly over a short period
questions.why: Offers such as discounts and free gifts give buyers a reason to buy now.

questions.q: A 'Buy two, get one free' offer is an example of
questions.why: It is a short-term incentive at the point of sale, a typical sales promotion technique.

questions.q: Which is an essential quality of a good salesperson?
questions.why: Product knowledge helps the salesperson answer questions and win the buyer's trust.

questions.q: Which of these is a consumer-oriented sales promotion?
questions.why: Free samples are given to consumers; the others are aimed at dealers or the sales force.

questions.q: The main advantage of personal selling is that
o: its cost per customer is very low
face-to-face, two-way talk lets doubts be cleared on the spot
it reaches millions of people at once
questions.why: Personal selling is flexible and interactive, though costly and limited in reach.

long.q: Explain any four techniques of consumer sales promotion.
scheme: B1: Free samples: small quantities given free so buyers can try the product.
B1: Discounts / price-off: goods sold below the usual price for a short time.
B1: Coupons: vouchers giving a stated amount off the price.
B1: Premium/bonus offers or contests: extra quantity or a gift with the product, or prizes in a contest.

long.q: Distinguish between advertising and personal selling on two bases.
scheme: B1: Contact: advertising is non-personal, through media; personal selling is face-to-face.
B1: Reach and cost: advertising reaches a large audience at a low cost per person; personal selling reaches few people at a high cost per person.

long.q: State three qualities of a good salesperson.
scheme: B1: Good knowledge of the product and of the firm.
B1: Pleasant manners, patience and good communication skills.
B1: Honesty, self-confidence and the ability to understand customers' needs.

long.q: Give two limitations of sales promotion.
scheme: B1: Its effect is short-lived; sales may fall once the offer ends.
B1: Too many offers may make buyers doubt the product's quality or wait for discounts.

long.q: A store in Chandigarh offers 'Flat 20% off' on a jacket marked ₹2,500, and accepts a ₹200 coupon after the discount. (a) Find what the buyer pays. (b) Name the two sales promotion techniques used.
scheme: A1: Price after discount = ₹2,000.
A1: Amount paid after the coupon = ₹2,000 − ₹200 = ₹1,800.
B1: (b) Price-off (discount) offer and coupon.

questions.q: A brand is
o: a name, sign, symbol or design that identifies a seller's product
the price written on the product
the factory where the product is made
a tax paid on the product
questions.why: A brand distinguishes one seller's goods from those of competitors.

questions.q: A brand name or mark registered under law so that others cannot use it is called
questions.why: A registered trademark gives the owner legal protection; a patent protects an invention.

questions.q: Which detail must appear on the label of packaged goods sold in India?
questions.why: Packaged-goods rules require details such as MRP, net quantity, the maker's name and the date of manufacture.

questions.q: Which is an example of primary packaging?
o: The cardboard box around the toothpaste tube
The truck that delivers the cartons
questions.why: Primary packaging is the immediate container; the box is secondary and the carton is transport packaging.

questions.q: Which is a function of packaging?
o: Protecting the product from damage and contamination
questions.why: Packaging protects, stores and helps sell the product; it does not fix prices or pay taxes.

long.q: State two advantages of branding to the manufacturer and two to the consumer.
scheme: B1: Manufacturer: distinguishes its product from rivals and builds customer loyalty.
B1: Manufacturer: makes advertising easier and allows a slightly higher price for a trusted brand.
B1: Consumer: easy to identify and ask for the product.
B1: Consumer: assures consistent quality and gives a sense of trust.

long.q: Explain any three functions of a label.
scheme: B1: Identifies the product and the brand.
B1: Describes the product: contents, quantity, MRP, dates of manufacture and expiry, instructions for use.
B1: Helps promotion through attractive design, and meets legal requirements.

long.q: Explain primary, secondary and transportation packaging, giving one example of each.
scheme: B1: Primary packaging: the immediate container of the product.
B1: Example: a bottle of cough syrup.
B1: Secondary packaging: an extra layer that protects and displays the primary pack.
B1: Example: the cardboard box in which the syrup bottle is sold.
B1: Transportation packaging: packing used to store and carry goods in bulk.
B1: Example: a large corrugated carton holding 50 such boxes.

long.q: State two qualities of a good brand name.
scheme: B1: Short, simple and easy to pronounce and remember.
B1: Distinctive and suggestive of the product's benefit, and able to be registered legally.

long.q: Why is packaging called a 'silent salesman'?
scheme: B1: An attractive pack catches the buyer's eye on the shelf, especially in self-service stores.
B1: Its design and information persuade the buyer without any salesperson speaking.

questions.q: Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, who is NOT a consumer?
o: A person who buys a refrigerator for home use
A person who buys goods in order to resell them
A person who hires a taxi
A person who buys a phone online for personal use
questions.why: The Act excludes those who buy goods for resale or other commercial purposes.

questions.q: The consumer's 'right to be heard' means that
o: the consumer's complaints will receive due consideration at appropriate forums
the consumer may shout at shopkeepers
every advertisement must be read aloud
the consumer can fix the price of goods
questions.why: It assures consumers that their interests and grievances will be considered.

questions.q: The three-tier machinery for settling consumer disputes consists of
o: Police station, High Court and Supreme Court
District, State and National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions
questions.why: Consumer disputes are heard by commissions at district, state and national levels.

questions.q: The ISI mark on a product shows that
o: it is agricultural produce such as honey or ghee
it shows how energy-efficient an appliance is
it is an industrial product that meets the standards of the Bureau of Indian Standards
it is a vegetarian food item
questions.why: ISI is the BIS mark for industrial goods; AGMARK is for farm produce and star labels show energy efficiency.

questions.q: Which is a responsibility of a consumer?
o: Asking for a proper bill (cash memo) for every purchase
questions.why: A bill is proof of purchase and is needed to make a complaint.

long.q: Explain any four rights of consumers.
scheme: B1: Right to safety: protection against goods and services that are hazardous to life and property.
B1: Right to be informed: about quality, quantity, price, ingredients and expiry.
B1: Right to choose: access to a variety of goods at competitive prices.
B1: Right to seek redressal (or to be heard, or to consumer education): to get relief against unfair practices.

long.q: State three responsibilities of consumers.
scheme: B1: Buy standardised goods (ISI, AGMARK, hallmark) and check quality, quantity and expiry.
B1: Insist on a proper bill and keep the warranty card.
B1: File a complaint for genuine grievances and be aware of their rights.

long.q: State two ways in which consumers may be exploited.
scheme: B1: Adulteration of goods, or under-weighing and short measures.
B1: Charging more than the MRP, selling expired goods, or making false claims in advertisements.

long.q: Neha bought a mixer-grinder in Lucknow with a one-year warranty. It stopped working after three months, and the dealer refused to repair it. (a) Which consumer right is involved? (b) Where can she complain? (c) What documents should she keep? (d) State two reliefs she may get.
scheme: B1: (a) The right to seek redressal.
B1: (b) The District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission.
B1: (c) The bill (cash memo) and the warranty card.
B1: (d) Free repair or replacement of the mixer-grinder.
B1: (d) Refund of the price, or compensation for loss and inconvenience.

long.q: Explain how the standard marks ISI, AGMARK and Hallmark protect consumers.
scheme: B1: ISI: certifies that industrial products such as electrical goods meet BIS standards, so they are safe.
B1: AGMARK: certifies the quality and purity of agricultural products such as ghee, honey and spices.
B1: Hallmark: certifies the purity of gold and silver jewellery.

questions.q: Fixed capital is invested in
o: long-term assets such as land, buildings and machinery
questions.why: Fixed capital is tied up in assets used over many years.

questions.q: Net working capital equals
questions.why: Net working capital is the excess of current assets over current liabilities.

questions.q: Compared with a manufacturing firm of the same size, a trading firm usually needs
o: less fixed capital and relatively more working capital
more fixed capital and no working capital
questions.why: A trader needs no heavy machinery but must hold stock and give credit.

questions.q: Which of these increases a firm's need for working capital?
o: Selling goods to customers on long credit
questions.why: Long credit to customers locks up funds in debtors; buying on credit reduces the need.

questions.q: A firm has current assets of ₹4,20,000 and current liabilities of ₹2,80,000. Its net working capital is

long.q: Distinguish between fixed capital and working capital on any three bases.
scheme: B1: Meaning: fixed capital is invested in long-term assets; working capital finances day-to-day operations.
B1: Examples: land, building, machinery for fixed capital; stock, debtors, cash for working capital.
B1: Period: fixed capital is locked up for a long time.
B1: Working capital keeps circulating in the short term (cash → stock → debtors → cash).
B1: Source: fixed capital comes from long-term sources (shares, debentures, long-term loans).
B1: Working capital comes mainly from short-term sources (trade credit, overdraft, cash credit).

long.q: State any four factors that determine the fixed capital needed by a business.
scheme: B1: Nature of business: manufacturing needs more than trading.
B1: Size or scale of operations.
B1: Technique of production: capital-intensive methods need more.
B1: Whether assets are bought or taken on lease/rent, and plans for growth.

long.q: From the following, calculate the net working capital: stock ₹85,000; debtors ₹60,000; cash ₹25,000; machinery ₹2,00,000; bills payable ₹30,000; creditors ₹70,000.
scheme: B1: Machinery is a fixed asset, so it is left out.

long.q: State two consequences of inadequate working capital.
scheme: B1: The firm cannot pay suppliers and wages on time, which harms its credit and goodwill.
B1: Production may stop for want of raw materials, and the firm misses cash discounts and good business chances.

long.q: Distinguish between gross working capital and net working capital.
scheme: B1: Gross working capital is the total of all current assets.
B1: Net working capital is current assets minus current liabilities.

questions.q: Which of these is an owners' fund for a company?
questions.why: Equity shareholders are the owners; the others are borrowed funds.

questions.q: Debenture holders receive
o: dividend only when there is profit
the remaining surplus after all claims
interest at a fixed rate, whether or not the company makes a profit
questions.why: Debentures are loans; interest is a charge on profit and must be paid.

questions.q: Which is a short-term source of finance?
questions.why: Trade credit from suppliers is usually for 30 to 90 days.

questions.q: Preference shareholders have priority over equity shareholders in
o: the payment of dividend and the return of capital on winding up
receiving fixed interest even in a loss
questions.why: They get dividend at a fixed rate before equity holders and are repaid capital first, but usually have limited voting rights.

questions.q: Retained earnings are
o: money raised by selling old machinery
profits kept in the business instead of being paid out as dividend
questions.why: Ploughing back profits is an internal source of finance.

long.q: Distinguish between shares and debentures on any three bases.
scheme: B1: Status: shareholders are owners of the company.
B1: Debenture holders are creditors (lenders) of the company.
B1: Return: shareholders get dividend, paid only out of profits.
B1: Debenture holders get fixed interest, payable even if there is no profit.
B1: Voting rights: equity shareholders have voting rights.
B1: Debenture holders have no voting rights; their money is usually secured on assets and repaid after a fixed period.

long.q: From the company's point of view, state two merits and two demerits of raising finance through equity shares.
scheme: B1: Merit: no fixed burden; dividend is paid only when there are profits.
B1: Merit: permanent capital that need not be repaid during the company's life.
B1: Demerit: issuing new shares dilutes the control of existing owners.
B1: Demerit: the cost of issue is high and dividend is not a tax-deductible expense.

long.q: Explain (a) trade credit and (b) bank overdraft as short-term sources of finance.
scheme: B1: (a) Trade credit: suppliers allow the firm to buy goods now and pay later.
B1: (a) Usually for a short period such as 30 to 90 days, without a formal loan.
B1: (b) Bank overdraft: the bank allows a current-account holder to withdraw more than the balance, up to a limit.
B1: (b) Interest is charged only on the amount overdrawn and for the period used.

long.q: A company has 50,000 equity shares of ₹10 each and 10,000 9% debentures of ₹100 each. Its profit before interest is ₹3,00,000. Ignoring tax, (a) find the debenture interest, (b) find the profit left for equity shareholders, (c) find the dividend per share if all of it is distributed, and (d) state why interest is paid before dividend.
scheme: A1: (a) Interest = ₹90,000.
B1: (d) Interest is a charge on profit owed to lenders; dividend is an appropriation of profit to owners.

long.q: Give two reasons why a company may prefer retained earnings to other sources of finance.
scheme: B1: No cost of issue and no fixed interest or repayment burden.
B1: Control of existing shareholders is not diluted, and funds are readily available.

topics.name: Final Accounts of a Sole Trader

questions.q: Gross profit is
o: net sales minus the cost of goods sold
questions.why: Gross profit comes from the Trading Account; net profit is found after indirect expenses.

questions.q: Which item is shown in the Trading Account?
questions.why: Carriage inwards is a direct expense of bringing goods in; carriage outwards is a selling expense in the Profit and Loss Account.

questions.q: Purchase of a new machine for the factory is
questions.why: It buys a fixed asset that will earn income for many years.

questions.q: Opening stock ₹20,000; purchases ₹80,000; closing stock ₹15,000; sales ₹1,10,000. Gross profit is
A Balance Sheet shows
o: the profit earned during the year
the financial position of the business on a particular date
questions.why: It lists assets, liabilities and capital at a point in time.

long.q: Prepare the Trading Account of Meena Stores and find the gross profit: opening stock ₹30,000; purchases ₹1,20,000; purchase returns ₹5,000; wages ₹15,000; carriage inwards ₹3,000; sales ₹2,10,000; sales returns ₹10,000; closing stock ₹40,000.
scheme: B1: Net purchases = ₹1,20,000 − ₹5,000 = ₹1,15,000 (debit side).
M1: Opening stock, wages and carriage inwards on the debit side (debit items total ₹1,63,000).
B1: Closing stock ₹40,000 on the credit side (credit total ₹2,40,000).

long.q: Distinguish between capital expenditure and revenue expenditure on two bases.
scheme: B1: Purpose: capital expenditure acquires or improves fixed assets (e.g. buying a van).
B1: Revenue expenditure meets day-to-day running costs (e.g. fuel for the van).
B1: Benefit and treatment: capital expenditure benefits many years and appears in the Balance Sheet.
B1: Revenue expenditure benefits only the current year and is charged to the Trading or Profit and Loss Account.

long.q: Gross profit ₹77,000; salaries ₹20,000; rent ₹12,000; carriage outwards ₹4,000; interest on loan ₹3,000; commission received ₹6,000. Calculate the net profit.
scheme: M1: Add indirect income: ₹77,000 + ₹6,000 = ₹83,000.
B1: Carriage outwards is a selling expense, so it goes to the Profit and Loss Account, not the Trading Account.

long.q: Classify each as capital or revenue expenditure: (a) wages paid to install a new machine, (b) repairs to the shop building, (c) purchase of a delivery van, (d) salaries of office staff.
scheme: B1: (a) Capital: installation cost is added to the cost of the machine.
B1: (b) Revenue.
B1: (c) Capital.
B1: (d) Revenue.

long.q: State two purposes of preparing a Balance Sheet.
scheme: B1: To show the financial position: what the business owns and owes on a date.
B1: To help owners, lenders and others judge its solvency and the owner's capital.

questions.q: The Reserve Bank of India is
o: a commercial bank owned by private shareholders
questions.why: The RBI, set up in 1935, regulates the banking system and the money supply.

questions.q: The repo rate is
o: the rate at which the RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks
the rate at which banks lend to the public
the interest paid on savings accounts
questions.why: Raising the repo rate makes borrowing costlier for banks, which helps control inflation.

questions.q: Which is a primary function of a commercial bank?
o: Paying insurance premiums on a customer's instruction
questions.why: Deposits and loans are primary functions; currency issue belongs to the RBI, and lockers or standing instructions are secondary functions.

questions.q: NEFT stands for
questions.why: NEFT is an RBI system for transferring money electronically between bank accounts.

questions.q: A cheque crossed 'A/c Payee only' means that
o: cash can be paid at the counter to anyone
the cheque can be transferred freely by endorsement
the amount can only be credited to the account of the named payee
the cheque has no expiry date
questions.why: This crossing directs the bank to credit only the payee's account, which makes the cheque safe.

long.q: Distinguish between the Reserve Bank of India and a commercial bank on two bases.
scheme: B1: Objective: the RBI regulates the banking and monetary system in the public interest and does not compete with banks.
B1: A commercial bank aims at earning profit.
B1: Customers: the RBI deals with the government and banks, and alone issues currency notes.
B1: Commercial banks deal with the general public.

long.q: Explain any four functions of the Reserve Bank of India.
scheme: B1: Issue of currency notes (except one-rupee notes and coins).
B1: Banker to the government: keeps its accounts and manages public debt.
B1: Bankers' bank: holds reserves of banks and lends to them as lender of last resort.
B1: Controller of credit (repo rate, CRR) and custodian of foreign exchange reserves.

long.q: Explain two agency functions of a commercial bank.
scheme: B1: Collecting cheques, dividends and interest on behalf of customers.
B1: Making payments such as insurance premiums, rent or loan instalments on standing instruction.

long.q: State three advantages of digital banking (such as UPI and net banking) and two precautions a user should take.
scheme: B1: Available 24 × 7 from anywhere.
B1: Instant, low-cost transfer of funds without visiting a branch.
B1: Less use of cash, and a clear record of every transaction.
B1: Precaution: never share your PIN, OTP or password with anyone.
B1: Precaution: use only official apps and secure networks, and check the payee before paying.

long.q: Distinguish between a savings account and a current account on two bases.
scheme: B1: Purpose: a savings account encourages saving by individuals and limits withdrawals.
B1: A current account suits businesses and allows any number of deposits and withdrawals.
B1: Interest: a savings account earns interest.
B1: A current account usually earns no interest but offers an overdraft facility.

questions.q: Recruitment means
o: choosing the best candidate from the applicants
searching for prospective employees and encouraging them to apply
questions.why: Recruitment builds a pool of applicants; selection then chooses from them.

questions.q: Which is an internal source of recruitment?
questions.why: Internal sources fill posts from within the organisation by promotion or transfer.

questions.q: The selection process ends with
o: issue of the appointment letter and placement on the job
questions.why: Selection moves from screening and tests to interviews, and ends with appointment and placement.

questions.q: Which is an example of on-the-job training?
o: A trainee working as an apprentice under an experienced worker
Studying case studies in a classroom
questions.why: On-the-job training is given at the workplace while doing the actual work.

questions.q: Induction (orientation) means
o: introducing a new employee to the organisation, colleagues and job
promoting an employee to a higher post
questions.why: Induction helps a new employee settle in and feel at home.

long.q: Distinguish between recruitment and selection on two bases.
scheme: B1: Meaning: recruitment searches for and attracts applicants; it comes first.
B1: Selection chooses the most suitable among them, using tests and interviews; it follows recruitment.
B1: Nature: recruitment is positive, as it increases the number of applicants.
B1: Selection is negative, as it rejects unsuitable candidates.

long.q: State two merits and one demerit of internal recruitment.
scheme: B1: Merit: motivates employees, since they see chances of promotion.
B1: Merit: cheaper and quicker; the employee already knows the organisation.
B1: Demerit: no fresh talent or new ideas come in, and choice is limited.

long.q: Explain any four steps in the selection process.
scheme: B1: Screening of applications and a preliminary interview.
B1: Selection tests (aptitude, skill or psychological tests).
B1: Employment interview to judge suitability.
B1: Reference checks and medical examination, followed by the appointment letter.

long.q: Distinguish between on-the-job and off-the-job training, giving one example of each.
scheme: B1: On-the-job training is given at the workplace while the employee does the job.
B1: Example: apprenticeship or coaching by a supervisor.
B1: Off-the-job training is given away from the workplace.
B1: Example: lectures, seminars, conferences or vestibule training.

long.q: State two benefits of training to employees and two to the organisation.
scheme: B1: Employees: improves skills and confidence.
B1: Employees: better chances of promotion and higher earnings.
B1: Organisation: higher productivity and quality, with less waste.
B1: Organisation: fewer accidents, less supervision needed and lower labour turnover.

questions.q: The main aim of public relations is to
o: keep the accounts of the firm
build and maintain goodwill between an organisation and its publics
questions.why: Public relations manages the organisation's image and relationships with all its publics.

questions.q: A press release is
o: a discount coupon printed in a newspaper
a written statement sent to the media announcing news about the organisation
a tax return filed with the government
a letter of appointment to a new employee
questions.why: Press releases give journalists the organisation's news in its own words.

questions.q: How does public relations differ from advertising?
o: Public relations is always paid space in newspapers
Public relations builds the organisation's image, while advertising directly promotes products
Public relations is used only by government offices
questions.why: Advertising is paid promotion of products; public relations works on reputation and goodwill, often through unpaid media coverage.

questions.q: Which activity is most likely to improve a company's public image?
o: Running free health camps and planting trees in local villages
Hiding information about a faulty product
questions.why: Social welfare activities (corporate social responsibility) earn public goodwill.

questions.q: When a company faces a crisis, such as a product recall, the best public relations step is
o: a prompt and honest statement to the media and customers
denying the problem until it is forgotten
removing all contact details from its website
questions.why: Quick, truthful communication protects trust; silence or denial damages the image further.

long.q: Explain any four functions of the public relations department of a company.
scheme: B1: Media relations: issuing press releases and holding press conferences.
B1: Building the company's image and goodwill among customers and society.
B1: Internal communication with employees through newsletters and meetings.
B1: Handling complaints and managing crises; organising social welfare (CSR) programmes.

long.q: Distinguish between public relations and advertising on two bases.
scheme: B1: Aim: public relations builds goodwill for the organisation; advertising promotes sales of products.
B1: Cost and control: advertising is paid and the firm controls the message; public relations often uses unpaid coverage the firm cannot fully control.

long.q: Name three tools of public relations.
scheme: B1: Press releases and press conferences.
B1: Sponsorship of events, sports or cultural programmes.
B1: House magazines or newsletters, exhibitions, open days or social welfare activities.

long.q: Some packets of a snack made by a food company were found contaminated in Chennai. Suggest four steps its public relations department should take.
scheme: B1: Issue a prompt, honest press statement admitting the problem.
B1: Recall the affected batch and offer refunds or replacements.
B1: Explain the steps taken to find the cause and prevent a repeat.
B1: Keep customers, dealers and employees informed through the media and social media until trust is rebuilt.

long.q: Explain 'internal publics' and 'external publics' of an organisation, giving two examples of each.
scheme: B1: Internal publics are people within the organisation.
B1: Examples: employees, managers, shareholders.
B1: External publics are people and groups outside it who are affected by it.
B1: Examples: customers, suppliers, media, government, local community.
